steps.explanationAfterStep: Methoxide removes an α-proton on the side away from the chlorine. (An enolate can also form on the chlorine side, but it cannot cyclise; it simply takes back a proton.)

The enolate carbon displaces chloride inside the molecule: a cyclopropanone forms, fused to a five-membered ring. The six-membered ring has already contracted. (The chloride may leave first, giving an oxyallyl cation that closes to the same cyclopropanone.)
Methoxide adds to the strained cyclopropanone. Changing the carbonyl carbon from sp² to sp³ relieves some of the angle strain.

The C=O bond re-forms, and the bond that breaks is a strained three-membered ring bond rather than the C–OMe bond: the product is an ester. The ring opens to give the more stable carbanion; here the two choices are the same.
The methanol made in the first step protonates the carbanion: methyl cyclopentanecarboxylate. The six-membered ring ketone has become a five-membered ring ester.

title: Favorskii rearrangement
subtitle: An α-chloroketone and methoxide: ring contraction through a cyclopropanone
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 36

enolate.caption: the enolate + methanol
hintTiers: The nucleophilic carbon of the enolate and the C–Cl carbon are both next to the carbonyl carbon. If they bond, how big is the new ring?
Chloride leaves as the enolate carbon bonds to the C–Cl carbon, and the oxygen lone pair re-forms C=O. Three arrows: a cyclopropanone forms.
C–Cl bond → a lone pair on chlorine; C=C π bond → new bond from the enolate carbon to the carbon that carried chlorine; oxygen lone pair → C=O π bond.
enolate.learnerPrompt: The enolate attacks the carbon carrying chlorine. Draw the ring closure.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The oxygen would make a strained three-membered ring with a C=C inside it. The enolate carbon attacks: a cyclopropanone forms.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right that chloride leaves. Now let the enolate C=C bond reach the carbon it left, and re-form the C=O bond.

products.caption: methyl cyclopentanecarboxylate + sodium chloride + sodium methoxide

carbanion.caption: a cyclopentyl carbanion carrying the ester
hintTiers: A carbanion is a strong base. Which molecule nearby can give it a proton?
The carbanion takes the drawn proton from methanol; the O–H pair stays on the methanol oxygen. Two arrows.
Carbanion lone pair → new bond to the H of methanol; that O–H bond → a lone pair on oxygen (methoxide is regenerated).

reactants.caption: 2-chlorocyclohexanone + sodium methoxide, in ether
hintTiers: Methoxide is a base. The α-hydrogens on the far side of the carbonyl group, away from the chlorine, can form an enolate that is set up to attack the C–Cl carbon. Which proton is that?
Methoxide takes the drawn α-hydrogen; the C–H pair makes a C=C bond and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Methoxide lone pair → new bond to the drawn H; that C–H bond → C=C π bond to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → a lone pair on oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Make an enolate on the side away from the chlorine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Direct SN2 displacement of chloride by methoxide gives 2-methoxycyclohexanone, a side product. The main reaction starts with an enolate on the other side of the carbonyl group.
Methoxide can add to the ketone, but that addition is reversible and leads nowhere yet. Deprotonate on the far side of the carbonyl group first.

cyclopropanone.caption: the cyclopropanone (bicyclo[3.1.0]hexan-6-one) + chloride
hintTiers: A cyclopropanone is very electrophilic: the sp² carbon is squeezed into a 60° angle. What does methoxide do to a reactive ketone?
The second methoxide adds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Methoxide lone pair → new bond to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → a lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Chloride is a weak nucleophile, and methoxide is present in excess. Methoxide attacks the strained carbonyl group.

tetrahedral-intermediate.caption: the tetrahedral intermediate
hintTiers: The oxygen anion can push back down to re-form C=O. Instead of methoxide leaving, a strained ring C–C bond can break. Where do its electrons go?
The oxygen lone pair re-forms C=O and one ring C–C bond of the carbonyl carbon breaks, its pair going to the ring carbon: a carbanion. Two arrows.
Oxygen lone pair → C=O π bond; a ring C–C bond of the carbonyl carbon → a lone pair on the other ring carbon.

misconceptions.arrowPattern: lp O2 -> π C1-O2; σ C1-O13 -> lp O13
misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing methoxide just goes back to the cyclopropanone. Breaking a strained ring bond instead is irreversible.
That bond does not belong to the carbonyl carbon, so the C=O cannot form. Break a bond from the carbonyl carbon to a ring carbon.

mechanismSummary: Methoxide forms the enolate of 2-chlorocyclohexanone on the side away from the chlorine. The enolate carbon displaces chloride inside the molecule, giving a strained cyclopropanone. Methoxide adds to its carbonyl group, and the tetrahedral intermediate collapses by breaking a ring C–C bond (not by losing methoxide), giving a carbanion that methanol protonates. The six-membered ring ketone becomes methyl cyclopentanecarboxylate.
